items.prompt: Why can a lunar eclipse only happen at full moon?

options.label: Because only at full moon does the Moon sit on the far side of Earth from the Sun, in the direction where Earth's shadow points
options.feedback: That exact position, opposite the Sun, is the only place in the Moon's orbit where Earth's shadow can ever reach it.

options.label: Because the Moon is closest to Earth at full moon
options.feedback: Distance from Earth doesn't follow the phase cycle this way. What matters is the Moon's position relative to the Sun and Earth, not how close it happens to be.

options.label: Because the Moon's own shadow can only reach Earth when it is full
options.feedback: A lunar eclipse is Earth's shadow falling on the Moon, not the other way round. The Moon's shadow falling on Earth is what makes a solar eclipse, and that needs new moon instead.

options.label: Because moonlight is strongest at full moon
options.feedback: Brightness doesn't create the alignment needed for an eclipse. Only the geometry of Sun, Earth and Moon lining up does that.

items.ok_line: Full moon is the one phase where the Moon sits inside the shadow Earth casts.
items.ko_line: Think about which single point in the Moon's orbit puts it opposite the Sun, in the direction Earth's shadow falls.
items.exp_title: Opposite the Sun, in the shadow's path
items.exp_text: Earth's shadow always points directly away from the Sun, stretching out into space on the side of Earth opposite the Sun. The Moon only enters that region of space when it is on the far side of Earth from the Sun, and that is precisely the arrangement that makes it look full. Every other phase places the Moon somewhere else entirely, well outside where Earth's shadow ever reaches.

items.prompt: If a lunar eclipse can only happen at full moon, why doesn't one happen every single full moon?

options.label: Because Earth's shadow is too small to reach the Moon most months
options.feedback: Earth's shadow easily reaches out well past the Moon's distance every month. It's the Moon missing the shadow's path, not the shadow falling short, that usually keeps it away.

options.label: Because the Moon's orbit is tilted slightly compared with Earth's path around the Sun, so most full moons pass just above or below Earth's shadow rather than through it
options.feedback: That small tilt is exactly why most full moons miss the shadow rather than pass through it.

options.label: Because the Moon skips some orbits around Earth
options.feedback: The Moon completes a full orbit every month without skipping. It's the alignment with the Sun and Earth, not the orbit itself, that varies.

options.label: Because the Sun blocks its own shadow most months
options.feedback: The Sun doesn't interfere with its own shadow. The miss happens because of the angle of the Moon's path, not anything the Sun does.

items.ok_line: The Moon's orbit doesn't lie flat against Earth's path around the Sun, so most full moons pass the shadow by.
items.ko_title: Not a small shadow, not a skipped orbit
items.ko_line: Earth's shadow is plenty large enough every month — think instead about whether the Moon's path actually crosses through it.
items.exp_text: Earth's shadow stretches far out into space every month, more than large enough to reach the Moon's distance without trouble. The Moon's orbit, however, is tilted by a small angle compared with the flat plane Earth's shadow lies in, so on most months the full moon passes a little above or a little below the shadow rather than through it. Only when a full moon happens to fall right where the Moon's tilted path crosses back through that flat plane does it actually pass into the shadow.

items.prompt: What is the difference between the umbra and the penumbra of Earth's shadow?

options.label: The umbra is the shadow's edge and the penumbra is its centre
options.feedback: That reverses the layout. The darkest, fully blocked region sits at the centre, with the partly lit zone forming a ring around it, not the other way round.

options.label: The umbra only exists during a solar eclipse, the penumbra only during a lunar eclipse
options.feedback: Earth casts both an umbra and a penumbra at all times, whether or not the Moon happens to be passing through either one.

options.label: The umbra is the dark core of the shadow where sunlight is completely blocked, while the penumbra is the lighter, surrounding zone where only part of the Sun is hidden
options.feedback: That split between a fully blocked core and a partly lit surrounding zone is exactly what separates the two.

options.label: The umbra is Earth's shadow and the penumbra is the Moon's own shadow
options.feedback: Both the umbra and the penumbra are parts of the same shadow, cast by Earth. The Moon's own shadow is a separate thing entirely, relevant only to a solar eclipse.

items.ok_line: Fully blocked at the core, only partly blocked around it.
items.ko_title: Not reversed, not two eclipses' worth
items.ko_line: Both zones belong to the very same shadow, cast by the very same object, at every moment, eclipse or not.
items.exp_title: Two zones of the one shadow
items.exp_text: Earth constantly casts a shadow out into space, and that shadow has two distinct parts. At its centre lies the umbra, where Earth completely blocks the Sun from view, and surrounding that core is the penumbra, a wider zone where Earth only blocks part of the Sun, leaving the rest still shining through. Which of the two the Moon passes through, or whether it passes through both, is what decides how the eclipse turns out.

items.prompt: What decides whether a lunar eclipse turns out total, partial, or merely penumbral?

options.label: How far away the Moon is from Earth that month
options.feedback: Distance changes the Moon's apparent size only slightly. The type of eclipse instead comes from how close the Moon's path passes to the very centre of Earth's shadow.

options.label: How many hours the eclipse lasts
options.feedback: Duration is a result of the path the Moon takes through the shadow, not the cause that decides which type of eclipse is happening.

options.label: Whether the eclipse happens during the day or night where you are
options.feedback: A lunar eclipse looks the same everywhere it's visible at once. Local time of day only decides whether you can see it, not which type it is.

options.label: How deep into Earth's umbra the Moon passes: fully inside makes it total, partly inside makes it partial, and only inside the outer penumbra makes it penumbral
options.feedback: That depth of entry into the umbra is exactly what separates a total eclipse from a partial or a penumbral one.

items.ok_line: Straight through the dark core, partly through it, or only through the dim outer ring.
items.ko_title: Not distance, not duration, not time of day
items.ko_line: The type of eclipse is set before it even starts, by exactly where the Moon's path threads through the two zones of Earth's shadow.
items.exp_text: As the Moon crosses Earth's shadow, what matters is how much of the dark umbra it actually enters. If the whole Moon passes fully inside the umbra, the eclipse is total; if only part of the Moon reaches into the umbra while the rest stays in the penumbra, the eclipse is partial; and if the Moon's path only grazes the outer penumbra without ever touching the umbra, the eclipse is merely penumbral. The same shadow, entered at different depths, produces very different sights.

items.prompt: Why do lunar eclipses typically last far longer than solar eclipses?

options.label: Earth's shadow is much wider than the Moon, so the Moon takes a long time to cross all the way through it, while the Moon's much smaller shadow sweeps quickly past any single spot on Earth
options.feedback: That size difference between the two shadows is exactly what makes one so much slower to cross than the other.

options.label: Because the Moon moves more slowly during a lunar eclipse
options.feedback: The Moon's orbital speed doesn't change because of an eclipse. What differs is the size of the shadow it has to cross.

options.label: Because lunar eclipses happen closer to Earth
options.feedback: The distance between Earth and the Moon during an eclipse isn't unusual. The difference in duration comes from the size of the shadow being crossed, not distance.

options.label: Because clouds slow down how quickly a lunar eclipse is seen to progress
options.feedback: Clouds might block the view, but they have no effect on how long the Moon actually takes to cross Earth's shadow.

items.ok_line: The Moon has to travel a long way through a shadow far bigger than itself.
items.ko_title: Not speed, not distance, not clouds
items.ko_line: The Moon's own speed hasn't changed — think about the size of what it's crossing compared with what a solar eclipse's shadow has to cross.
items.exp_title: A small shadow versus a big one
items.exp_text: Earth's shadow is many times wider than the Moon, so once the Moon begins entering it, a long stretch of orbit still has to be covered before it comes out the other side. A solar eclipse works the other way around: it is the Moon's much smaller shadow that has to sweep across Earth, and any single spot on the ground passes through that narrow shadow in a short amount of time. Crossing a wide shadow simply takes longer than being brushed by a narrow one.

items.prompt: Why can an entire hemisphere of Earth watch the same lunar eclipse together, rather than only a narrow strip of land the way a solar eclipse works?

options.label: Because a lunar eclipse happens closer to Earth's surface
options.feedback: The Moon's distance from Earth doesn't change because of an eclipse. Visibility instead comes down to what is actually being blocked, and where.

options.label: Because the eclipsed Moon is a single object visible to everyone on Earth's night side at once, unlike a solar eclipse where the Moon's small shadow only covers a narrow strip of ground
options.feedback: Being one single object out in space, rather than a shadow sweeping across the ground, is exactly why everyone on the night side can watch it together.

options.label: Because Earth's shadow moves across the ground the way the Moon's shadow does during a solar eclipse
options.feedback: It's the opposite case: Earth's shadow doesn't sweep across the ground at all here. The Moon itself sits far out in space and is simply visible, or not, from wherever it happens to be night.

options.label: Because a lunar eclipse only happens over oceans, where more people can see it
options.feedback: A lunar eclipse isn't tied to any particular geography. Wherever the Moon is above the horizon and it's night, the eclipse is visible.

items.ok_line: Everyone on the night side is looking at the same Moon at the same time.
items.ko_title: Not closer, not a moving shadow on the ground
items.ko_line: Nothing about a lunar eclipse changes the Moon's distance, and no shadow sweeps across Earth's surface here at all.
items.exp_title: Watching the same object, not a shadow crossing the ground
items.exp_text: During a lunar eclipse, what is blocked is sunlight reaching the Moon itself, far out in space, not sunlight reaching any particular patch of Earth's surface. Since the Moon is a single object, anyone anywhere on the night side of Earth can simply look up and see the same eclipsed Moon at the same moment. A solar eclipse works in reverse, with the Moon's small shadow sweeping across Earth's surface and only briefly touching a narrow strip of ground at any one time.

items.prompt: Why is it safe to look directly at a lunar eclipse with the naked eye, when looking at a solar eclipse can damage your eyes?

options.label: Because the Moon blocks all of the Sun's harmful light during a lunar eclipse
options.feedback: There is no direct sunlight involved in watching a lunar eclipse at all. You are looking at the Moon at night, not anywhere near the Sun in the sky.

options.label: Because a lunar eclipse only lasts a few seconds
options.feedback: A lunar eclipse actually runs for a long stretch of time. How long you look has nothing to do with why it is safe.

options.label: A lunar eclipse only involves looking at the Moon's reflected light, which is far too dim to harm the eyes, unlike looking directly at the Sun's own light during a solar eclipse
options.feedback: That dim, reflected light, nothing at all like looking towards the Sun, is exactly why there is nothing here to harm the eyes.

options.label: Because eclipses in general are always safe to view directly
options.feedback: A solar eclipse is the clear exception, dangerous specifically because it involves looking towards the direct light of the Sun itself.

items.ok_title: Reflected light, not the Sun itself
items.ok_line: You are looking at moonlight, and moonlight was never bright enough to hurt your eyes.
items.ko_line: No sunlight is anywhere near your line of sight during a lunar eclipse — you are looking at night, towards the Moon, not towards the Sun.
items.exp_text: Watching a lunar eclipse means looking at the Moon at night, seeing only the faint sunlight it reflects back towards Earth, and that reflected glow is far too weak to cause any damage. A solar eclipse is dangerous for the opposite reason: it means looking almost directly at the Sun itself, whose direct light can harm the eyes whether or not part of it happens to be covered. The two events only share the word 'eclipse' — what you are actually looking at is completely different in each case.

items.prompt: Why is a penumbral lunar eclipse often so subtle that most people never notice it happening?

options.label: Because penumbral eclipses only happen during the day
options.feedback: A penumbral eclipse follows the same full-moon timing as any other lunar eclipse and is visible at night. What makes it subtle is how little of the Moon's light is actually blocked.

options.label: Because the Moon is unusually far from Earth during a penumbral eclipse
options.feedback: Distance isn't what sets a penumbral eclipse apart. It's about how much of the shadow the Moon actually passes through.

options.label: Because clouds usually cover penumbral eclipses
options.feedback: Weather is unrelated to why the effect itself is faint. Even under a clear sky, a penumbral eclipse produces only a slight, easy-to-miss dimming.

options.label: The Moon only passes through the outer penumbra, where part of the Sun is still visible from the Moon's surface, so it only dims slightly instead of losing its light
options.feedback: Only dimming slightly, rather than truly darkening, is exactly what happens when the Moon never reaches the fully blocked umbra.

items.ok_title: Barely inside the shadow at all
items.ok_line: Only the faint outer ring, where the Sun is merely dimmed, never truly hidden.
items.ko_title: Not daytime, not distance, not weather
items.ko_line: A penumbral eclipse follows full moon like any other; what makes it hard to notice is how little of the Sun actually gets blocked.
items.exp_title: A shadow too shallow to show
items.exp_text: In the outer penumbra, Earth only blocks part of the Sun's disc as seen from the Moon, so sunlight keeps reaching the Moon's surface, just slightly reduced rather than cut off. Because human eyes are not very good at noticing a small drop in brightness, especially against a Moon that is already just reflected light, the dimming during a penumbral eclipse often passes completely unnoticed. Only when the Moon dips into the fully dark umbra does the change become obvious enough to see.

items.prompt: Why do a lunar eclipse and a solar eclipse often occur within about two weeks of each other?

options.label: Both need the Moon to be near the same crossing point of its tilted orbit, and the Moon reaches a full moon and a new moon roughly two weeks apart during that same window
options.feedback: Sharing that same brief crossing window, with a full moon and a new moon falling inside it two weeks apart, is exactly why the pair shows up so close together.

options.label: Because one eclipse directly causes the other to happen
options.feedback: Neither eclipse causes the other. Both are separate results of the same alignment window, not one triggering the next.

options.label: Because the Sun moves quickly enough to set up both eclipses in that time
options.feedback: The Sun's apparent motion across our sky is far too slow to explain a gap of only two weeks. The timing instead comes from the Moon's own faster movement between phases.

options.label: It's a coincidence with no shared cause
options.feedback: The pairing is regular and predictable, not a coincidence. Both eclipses depend on the same brief stretch of time when the Moon's tilted orbit crosses Earth's path around the Sun.

items.ok_line: One tilted-orbit crossing, and both a full moon and a new moon fall within it.
items.ko_title: Not cause and effect, not coincidence
items.ko_line: Neither eclipse triggers the other — both are separate results of the same brief alignment.
items.exp_text: Both a lunar eclipse and a solar eclipse require the Moon to be near the point where its tilted orbit crosses the flat plane of Earth's path around the Sun. That crossing stays lined up with the Sun for only a few weeks at a time, and within that same short window the Moon passes through both a full moon and a new moon, since it does so every month regardless. When the timing lines up, one of those phases brings a lunar eclipse and the other brings a solar eclipse, back to back.

items.prompt: What is true about the ocean tides on the day of a lunar eclipse?

options.label: The eclipse itself pulls extra water toward the Moon
options.feedback: Blocking sunlight from reaching the Moon doesn't change the Moon's gravity or its pull on Earth's oceans at all.

options.label: Since a lunar eclipse can only happen at full moon, it always coincides with a spring tide, the especially large swing between high and low water caused by the Sun and Moon lining up
options.feedback: That full-moon timing, which always lines up the Sun and Moon, is exactly what a spring tide requires as well.

options.label: Tides pause briefly during a lunar eclipse
options.feedback: The tides keep rising and falling on their usual schedule throughout an eclipse. Nothing about the Moon passing through Earth's shadow interrupts that rhythm.

options.label: Lunar eclipses always coincide with unusually small, neap tides
options.feedback: Neap tides happen near the quarter moons, roughly a week away from full moon. A lunar eclipse, tied to full moon, lines up with the opposite case instead.

items.ok_line: Full moon means Sun and Moon in line, and that line-up is what spring tides are.
items.ko_title: Not extra pull, not paused, not neap
items.ko_line: The eclipse changes what you can see of the Moon, not what its gravity is doing to the ocean.
items.exp_title: The tide was already set by the phase
items.exp_text: A lunar eclipse can only happen at full moon, and a full moon always means the Sun, Earth and Moon are lined up in roughly a straight row. That same alignment is exactly what produces a spring tide, the especially large swing between high and low water, regardless of whether an eclipse happens to be taking place. The eclipse itself changes nothing about the Moon's gravity or the ocean; it simply happens to land on a day when the tide was already set up for its familiar spring-tide swing.
